_comment:
Who actually sponsors H-1B workers: the staffing and consulting trade.

WHY THIS EXISTS. The published lists of "top employers" are Amazon, Google and
Microsoft, which is what a reader of the news sees. They are not where the
volume sits. This reads every row USCIS publishes -- fifteen fiscal years of
its H-1B Employer Data Hub, one row per employer per year -- and separates the
firms whose business IS supplying workers from the firms that hire them for
themselves, using the employer's own NAICS code rather than a guess from its
name.

WHAT IT MEASURES, AND WHAT EACH FIGURE MEANS.
  * INITIAL approvals are new workers entering the programme; CONTINUING
    approvals are extensions and amendments for someone already in it. They
    must never be summed: the same person appears again every time their
    petition is renewed. The ratio between them is itself the signal --
    a firm with many continuing approvals per initial one is holding workers
    over years, which is what a staffing arrangement looks like.
  * The DENIAL rate is USCIS's own, per employer and year.
  * INDUSTRY, as far as the hub goes. Every row carries a NAICS code of
    exactly two digits -- "54", "56" -- which is a sector, not an industry:
    "54" holds law firms, engineering consultancies and IT consultancies
    alike. A staffing agency CANNOT be separated from its clients here. That
    classification needs the Labor Department's disclosure files, which carry
    six digits plus the employer's own dependency and third-party-placement
    answers; it is done in build_visa_bodyshops.py, and this file's job is
    the thing the hub does better than anything else -- counting approved
    people, by employer, over fifteen years.

WHO IS BARRED. The Labor Department's debarment lists are joined on the
employer name (data/policy/debarments.json, verified against the live DOL
pages). Two things about that list matter more than its contents: it is very
short, and a SUSPENSION pending investigation -- the action reported against
Cloudera and Cognizant -- never appears on it at all, because DOL publishes
no list of suspensions.

suspensions.claim: Cognizant was blocked from filing new PERM applications pending an investigation; existing H-1B visas and approved labor certifications remain valid; triggered by whistleblower complaints and a White House fraud task force.
suspensions.verdict: PARTIALLY VERIFIED — no primary DOL/OFLC instrument found. The only primary-source record located is public statements by the DOL Inspector General (official @DOLOIG / Anthony P. D'Esposito X account) on September 8, 2026. There is NO DOL news release, NO OFLC announcement on dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/news or flag.dol.gov/announcements, NO Federal Register document, and NO located court/OCAHO filing naming Cognizant. Cognizant does NOT appear on any published OFLC or WHD debarment list. The 'existing visas/certifications remain valid' and 'whistleblower complaints' details are reported by secondary media only and are not stated in any primary document found.
suspensions.evidence: DOL OIG press release of July 8, 2026 is the primary record of the underlying investigation: 'The U.S. Department of Labor, Office of Inspector General (OIG), today launched a major investigation and is intensifying enforcement efforts to combat fraud and human trafficking in the H-1B and Program Electronica Review Management (PERM) systems. Working alongside federal law enforcement partners and President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance's Taks Force to Eliminate Fraud...' It names NO companies and announces NO suspension of filings. The September 8, 2026 action was announced by IG D'Esposito on X ('Cognizant. Cloudera. H1-B processing suspended.'), reported by Business Standard, Epoch Times, Newsweek and others. Distinction: this is a SUSPENSION PENDING INVESTIGATION, not a debarment; suspensions do not appear on the published debarment lists.
suspensions.date: OIG investigation announced July 8, 2026; Cognizant PERM suspension announced by IG on X September 8, 2026

suspensions.claim: Cloudera was blocked from filing new PERM applications pending an investigation.
suspensions.verdict: VERIFIED for a May 12, 2026 PERM suspension via an official DOL news release (a distinct, earlier action from the September 8, 2026 IG announcement). The September 8, 2026 extension to H-1B processing rests only on the IG's X statements, with no primary DOL instrument found.
suspensions.evidence: DOL news release, May 12, 2026: 'US departments of Labor, Justice announce enforcement actions against Cloudera Inc. for alleged Immigration and Nationality Act violations.' The Employment and Training Administration's Office of Foreign Labor Certification suspended processing of all permanent labor certification applications filed by, or on behalf of, Cloudera for 180 days, extendable pending the outcome of the DOJ investigation. This followed a DOJ Civil Rights Division (Immigrant and Employee Rights Section) lawsuit filed April 28, 2026 before the Office of the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer (OCAHO), alleging Cloudera created a non-functional recruitment email address so U.S. workers could not apply, then certified to ETA that no qualified U.S. workers were available. This is a SUSPENSION under OFLC's existing suspension authority, not a debarment. Cloudera does NOT appear on any published debarment list.
suspensions.date: DOJ complaint filed April 28, 2026; DOL/OFLC 180-day PERM suspension announced May 12, 2026

no_list_published.item: Employers barred from H-1B/STEM OPT sponsorship
no_list_published.finding: No USCIS-published list of barred employers exists. USCIS acts on DOL debarments: under 8 CFR 214.1/20 CFR part 655, 'upon debarment by the Department of Labor pursuant to 20 CFR part 655, USCIS may deny any petition filed by that petitioner for nonimmigrant status under section 101(a)(15)(H)... for a period of at least 1 year but not more than 5 years.' The operative public list remains DOL's.

no_list_published.item: Employers barred or suspended from SEVP / STEM OPT
no_list_published.finding: No such public list is published. SEVP's most recent relevant document, Broadcast Message 2603-02 'STEM OPT Employer Fraud' (March 23, 2026), warns DSOs about fraud among 'IT recruitment, consulting firms, and staffing agencies' and lists fraud indicators from site visits, but names no employers and references no list of barred employers. SEVP decertifies SCHOOLS, not employers; there is no employer debarment mechanism in the SEVP/OPT regulations. STEM OPT employer eligibility turns on E-Verify good standing, and USCIS publishes no list of E-Verify participants either.

no_list_published.item: Separate WHD public enforcement dataset of H-1B debarments
no_list_published.finding: WHD's H-1B debarment list IS the WHD enforcement product (the page is on dol.gov/agencies/whd). The separate WHD enforcement database (enforcedata.dol.gov) carries H-1B investigation case data with back-wage and civil-money-penalty amounts but does not publish debarment start/end dates; the debarment page is authoritative for those.

no_list_published.item: Published list of employers SUSPENDED (as opposed to debarred) pending investigation
no_list_published.finding: None exists. OFLC publishes debarments only. Suspensions under OFLC's suspension authority (as applied to Cloudera, and as reported for Cognizant) are announced ad hoc by press release or not at all, and do not appear on any list. This is why Cognizant and Cloudera are absent from the debarment lists despite the reported actions.

caveats: Every hub row carries a two-digit NAICS sector and nothing finer, so no count here separates a staffing firm from the companies it supplies.
The hub names an employer per fiscal year; a firm that renames or splits entities appears as more than one employer.
Debarment is a formal bar with dates. A suspension pending investigation is not published in any list, so absence from these lists is not evidence of good standing.

Retrieved 2026-09-15. www.dol.gov blocks command-line clients via Akamai (HTTP 403); pages were retrieved through a browser-equivalent fetcher, which returns the debarments page as a print-rendered PDF. Content was cross-checked by two independent fetches for the H-1B list.

There is no separate OFLC-issued H-1B/LCA debarment list. The OFLC debarments page defers entirely to WHD: 'The link below is to a list of employers debarred or disqualified by the Wage and Hour Division. The Office of Foreign Labor Certification... will not accept for filing any application or attestation submitted by these employers under 20 CFR Part 656 or 20 CFR subparts A, B, C, D, E, H, or I. (See, 20 CFR 655.750(d); 20 CFR 655.855(d).)'

DATA-QUALITY FINDING: the downloadable worksheet linked from the WHD H-1B debarment page (https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WHD/legacy/files/H1BDebarmentList.xls) is STALE. Its internal footer reads '(EFFECTIVE May 1, 2024)' and 'Last Updated on April 30, 2024', and the file's OLE metadata shows it was last saved 2024-03-31. It contains a completely different, now-expired roster (Broadgate, Inc.; Macks USA, Inc. and Mujeeb Rahman, Individually; Packet One, LLC; Virtulytix, Inc.; BER-IT, Inc.; Bonzer, LLC; Amica Technology Solutions, LLC) and shares no entries with the current HTML table. Anyone scripting against the .xls would get a roster over two years out of date. The HTML table is authoritative.

The H-1B list publishes no employer addresses: an 'Employer Address' column exists in the table structure but is empty for all five current entries. The list also carries no stated violation basis beyond the 'Willful Violator' flag (all five are flagged Yes); WHD refers readers to Fact Sheet #62S for the definition of a willful violator employer.

SCALE OF DEBARRED EMPLOYERS: the debarment lists are populated almost entirely by very small entities. All five current H-1B debarments are small firms — two are Florida private schools (Sherwood Academy in Mount Dora; Da Vinci Academy in Hunters Creek/Orlando) and three are small IT/staffing-type companies. No large-cap or well-known corporation appears on any of the four lists. The H-2A and H-2B lists are dominated by individual farm labor contractors, single-site farms, landscapers, restaurants, hotels and small construction firms; 13 of the 56 H-2B entries are Guam-based individuals or small companies. The PERM list has just two names, one of them an individual agent. The large firms named in 2026 enforcement news (Cognizant, Cloudera) appear on NO list. The reported action in each case was a suspension pending investigation rather than a debarment, and suspensions are published nowhere.

DEBARMENT vs SUSPENSION: a debarment is a formal bar for a fixed period (or permanent) and is published on these lists. A suspension pending investigation is temporary, is imposed under OFLC's separate suspension authority, and is NOT published on any list. All five named H-1B companies are debarments. The 2026 reports about Cognizant and Cloudera describe suspensions rather than debarments, which is consistent with their absence from these lists -- but absence from a list is not itself evidence of a suspension, and the verified standing of each report differs. See the entry for each.

Four entries across the lists are PERMANENT debarments: International Labor Management Corporation (ILMC) of Vass, NC (on both H-2A and H-2B, from August 1, 2014, by plea agreement in the US District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina); Michael Wayne Butikofer of Monon, Iowa (on both H-2A and H-2B, plea agreement, no start date printed); and on H-2B, four Guam entities/individuals — Acme Universal Inc., Dai Wang, Maria Teresa Gozum and Xin Bo 'Paul' Yu — listed as 'Permanent' with no end date.

Several entries on the OFLC lists contain typographical errors in the source, transcribed here verbatim: El Carreton end date 'August 30. 2027'; Zimmerman Restaurant end date 'July,10, 2030'; Tex-Mex Trucking end date 'September 28 2027'; Cantu Harvesting start February 28, 2024 with end February 20, 2027; Gumara Canela start January 15, 2026 with end January 16, 2029; Jorel/Scott/Selina/Shaolin Tereas and Tereas, Inc. start January 28, 2026 with end January 29, 2028; Jevon Natali has a start date of November 1, 2026 (in the future relative to retrieval) with end October 31, 2027; Maria Esther Gamas-Perez shows a one-year term (March 22, 2026 to March 22, 2027) against the three-year norm. The July 8, 2026 OIG press release also contains two errors in the source: 'Program Electronica Review Management' (PERM is Program Electronic Review Management) and 'Taks Force'.

Expired debarments are published separately by OFLC: 'Expired H-2A Debarments, FY 2014-current' and 'Expired H-2B Debarments, FY2014-current' are linked from the debarments page. No expired-debarment archive is published for H-1B or PERM.

OFLC also points to a related but distinct WHD list: ineligible Farm Labor Contractors under the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act (MSPA), at https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/agriculture/mspa/farm-labor-contractors/. This is an MSPA registration list, not a visa-programme debarment list.

A Federal Register full-text search for Cognizant and Cloudera in connection with labor certification returned zero documents. No rulemaking or Federal Register notice was found for either action. A search that finds nothing is not proof that nothing exists.
